analysis.one_liner: Exempts Alaska's national forests from the Roadless Rule, which currently bars roads and logging there.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, where it sat with no further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Roadless Rule is a federal regulation that bars building new roads and doing most logging in designated roadless areas of national forests, including about 9 million acres in Alaska. This bill would have wiped that rule off the books for every acre of national forest land in Alaska, freeing those areas for road construction and timber harvesting. It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee on the day it was introduced and never moved again; it got no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would have been Alaska's timber and logging industry, which would gain access to roadless national forest land for roads and harvest. Road construction and development interests would also gain access to areas currently closed off.

how_it_helps.text: By voiding the Roadless Rule's application in Alaska, the bill would permit road construction and logging in National Forest roadless areas, opening timber resources and access that the rule currently blocks.

analysis.who_pays: The cost would fall on the public's shared resources: roughly 9 million acres of roadless national forest in Alaska, used for hunting, fishing, and recreation, would be opened to roads and logging, and taxpayers would bear the cost of subsidized road-building in remote forest land.
analysis.who_pays_short: Alaska's public forests and their users

drawbacks.text: The bill would remove federal protection from about 9 million acres of inventoried roadless national forest land in Alaska, allowing road construction and timber harvesting in areas currently off-limits under the Roadless Rule.

Because the exemption is written as a flat exemption from the rule for all Alaska national forest land, it leaves no mechanism to limit which roadless areas could be developed, unlike the more targeted case-by-case processes some states have used.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was never enacted, so its tradeoffs were never tested legislatively. Had it passed, it would have opened roughly 9 million acres of protected national forest in Alaska to road-building and logging, which supporters argued would create jobs in struggling rural communities; opponents would have countered that it sacrificed a widely valued public resource for a small regional industry. As it stands, the main fact is that a two-sentence bill referencing no numbers died with no committee action, no votes, and no debate.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a vote, or a way to the floor before Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 13, 2011 by Senator Begich and read twice before being referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.
No further action was ever taken: the action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor consideration before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.
The bill carried only one cosponsor, Senator Murkowski of Alaska.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The nearly 9 million acres of roadless national forest in Alaska remain protected by the Roadless Rule, which continues to bar road construction and logging in those areas. The timber industry did not gain the access the bill would have provided.

for.name: Sen. Mark Begich
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it toward committee consideration.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors were Alaska senators from different parties (a Democrat and a Republican); no votes ever occurred, so the partisan shape of broader support or opposition cannot be measured from the record.

industries.note: Removing the Roadless Rule from Alaska's national forests would allow road construction and timber harvest in areas currently off-limits, expanding logging access.

industries.industry: Alaska tourism, fishing, and subsistence users
industries.note: These interests benefit economically from intact, roadless forests; lifting the rule could bring some access and jobs but risk the undeveloped character the tourism and fishing economies rely on.
